newsitem.title: UK: UK Treasury Committee urges further reforms at LSE.
newsitem.headline: UK Treasury Committee urges further reforms at LSE.

text.p: An influential British parliamentary committee on Thursday urged the London Stock Exchange (LSE) to give up its member club status and adopt a more open business structure.
The Treasury Select Committee, which has been critical of the way the exchange has been run, said the LSE would better reflect the interests of the market if it was not owned by member firms.
"We can see no reason why the Stock Exchange should now not develop a corporate structure," the Committee said in its report.
It added, "...We would not be surprised if the LSE came under further scrutiny from this Committee in the new Parliament."

The committee, which has been following developments at the exchange for about 18 months, said it was concerned that the LSE "remains so non-committal about the issue of ownership, particularly in the light of the increasingly competitive environment in which it finds itself."
Some market watchers say one option for the exchange is an eventual flotation.
An LSE spokeswoman said the issue of governance is "constantly under review," but the LSE has not specifically discussed a flotation.
"We have no plans now, but we're open to change," she said. "At the moment, we have a very full agenda so we probably won't be addressing it soon."
The Committee also urged Europe's biggest stock exchange to increase market transparency it launches its electronic order-driven order book in October 1997.
The LSE now uses a system under which share prices are set by primary dealers, known as market makers. It is the only major exchange where market makers set prices.

The LSE is still thrashing out the details of the new order-driven regime, and has put forth a controversial rule that would allow market makers to delay reporting large trades for the sake of market liquidity under the new order book regime.
"...We do not accept the view of the LSE that there is necessarily a trade off between transparency and liquidity," the committee reported.

It concluded, "...The LSE will be best served by ensuring that an effective, transparent order book -- with suitably formulated rules to allow a significant flow of business -- for the most liquid stocks is implemented as soon as possible ..." --London newsroom +44 171 542 5106
